claim: SlitOr5 is expressed with a more than 50-fold enrichment in male antennae compared to female antennae in S. littoralis.
source: We found SlitOr5 expressed with a more than 50-fold enrichment in the male antennae (Figure 1A), thus confirming previous observations (Legeai et al., 2011; Walker et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A and confirmed by previous studies cited.

claim: SlitOR5 belongs to a lineage distantly related to the type I PR clade.
source: Among the 20 paralogous lineages identified (each having evolved in principle from an ancestral OR present in the last common ancestor of Lepidoptera), SlitOR5 belonged to a lineage distantly related to the type I PR clade, as well as to the lineages containing type 0 and type II PRs (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SlitOR5-expressing OSNs strongly responded to (Z,E)-9,11-14:OAc in Drosophila heterologous expression system.
source: SlitOR5-expressing OSNs strongly responded to (Z,E)-9,11-14:OAc (65 ± 15 spikes.s−1), whereas there was no significant response to any other compound (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by single-sensillum recording data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SlitOR5 co-expressed with SlitOrco in Xenopus oocytes induced a strong current when stimulated with (Z,E)-9,11-14:OAc.
source: A strong current was induced in SlitOR5-expressing oocytes when stimulated with (Z,E)-9,11-14:OAc (3.9 ± 0.3 µA), whereas only minor currents were recorded in response to (Z,E)-9,12-14:OAc and (Z)9-12:OAc (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by two-electrode voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SlitOR5 has a low detection threshold of 10−8 M for (Z,E)-9,11-14:OAc.
source: SlitOR5 sensitivity was assessed with a dose-response experiment that showed a low detection threshold (10−8 M) and an EC50 of 1.707 × 10−7 M (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: Supported by dose-response experiments shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: SlitOR5 has an EC50 of 1.707 × 10−7 M for (Z,E)-9,11-14:OAc.
source: SlitOR5 sensitivity was assessed with a dose-response experiment that showed a low detection threshold (10−8 M) and an EC50 of 1.707 × 10−7 M (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: Supported by dose-response experiments shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: S. littoralis LT1A OSNs significantly responded to (Z,E)-9,11-14:OAc.
source: When stimulated with the 26 pheromone compounds, LT1A OSNs significantly responded to (Z,E)-9,11-14:OAc (55 ± 4 spikes.s−1) and to a lesser extent to its stereoisomer (Z,Z)-9,11-14:OAc, which is absent from any Spodoptera pheromone.
evidence: Supported by single-sensillum recordings on native S. littoralis OSNs.

claim: The response spectrum of heterologously expressed SlitOR5 mirrors that of S. littoralis LT1A OSNs.
source: This mirrored the response spectra of heterologously expressed SlitOR5, especially the one observed in Drosophila OSNs (Figure 2A).
evidence: Comparison of response spectra between heterologous expression and native OSNs.

claim: A 10 bp deletion was created in the first exon of SlitOr5 using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: We selected a line carrying a single mutation that consisted of a 10 bp deletion at the expected location, introducing a premature STOP codon within the SlitOr5 transcript after 247 codons (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by genotyping and sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The 10 bp deletion in SlitOr5 introduces a premature STOP codon after 247 codons.
source: We selected a line carrying a single mutation that consisted of a 10 bp deletion at the expected location, introducing a premature STOP codon within the SlitOr5 transcript after 247 codons (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Homozygous SlitOr5 mutant antennae showed no EAG response to (Z,E)-9,11-14:OAc.
source: When stimulated with (Z,E)-9,11-14:OAc, wild-type and SlitOr5+/- antennae exhibited similar EAG amplitudes (0.89 mV and 1.16 mV, respectively), whereas the response was completely abolished in SlitOr5-/- antennae (0.02 mV).
evidence: Supported by EAG recordings comparing wild-type, heterozygous, and homozygous mutants.

claim: Antennal responses to minor pheromone components and plant volatiles were not impaired in SlitOr5 mutants.
source: Control experiments using a S. littoralis minor pheromone component and plant volatiles known to induce EAG responses in S. littoralis (Saveer et al., 2012; López et al., 2017) showed that antennal responses were not impaired in SlitOr5-/- mutants, as these odorants elicited similar responses in wild-type, heterozygous and homozygous moths (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by EAG recordings with control odorants shown in Figure 3B and cited studies.

claim: More than 80% of wild-type males initiated movement toward the pheromone source in the first 8 minutes.
source: Whereas more than 80% of wild-type males initiated a movement toward the pheromone source in the first 8 min, only a minority of SlitOr5 mutants initiated such a movement (even after 30 min of test), a response similar to that of control wild-type males not stimulated with the pheromone (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Only a minority of SlitOr5 mutants initiated movement toward the pheromone source even after 30 minutes of testing.
source: Whereas more than 80% of wild-type males initiated a movement toward the pheromone source in the first 8 min, only a minority of SlitOr5 mutants initiated such a movement (even after 30 min of test), a response similar to that of control wild-type males not stimulated with the pheromone (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All steps of courtship behavior were affected in SlitOr5 mutants.
source: All the steps of the courtship behavior were similarly affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only 1 out of 13 SlitOr5 mutant males was able to mate with a wild-type virgin female.
source: When paired with a wild-type virgin female, only 1 out of the 13 SlitOr5-/- males tested was able to mate, compared to ~75% for wild-type males (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by mating experiment data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Approximately 75% of wild-type males were able to mate with a wild-type virgin female.
source: When paired with a wild-type virgin female, only 1 out of the 13 SlitOr5-/- males tested was able to mate, compared to ~75% for wild-type males (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by mating experiment data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SlitOR5 is the receptor responsible for the detection of the major component of the S. littoralis female pheromone blend.
source: Overall, these results confirm that SlitOR5 is the receptor responsible for the detection of the major component of the S. littoralis female pheromone blend.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from combined heterologous expression and loss-of-function studies.

claim: Lepidopteran ORs grouped within eight different paralogous lineages in the phylogenetic analysis.
source: ORs grouped within eight different paralogous lineages, four of which including PRs (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Four paralogous lineages include pheromone receptors.
source: ORs grouped within eight different paralogous lineages, four of which including PRs (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The PR clade contains all type I PRs characterized so far except SlitOR5.
source: One was the so-called PR clade that, as previously observed, contained all type I PRs characterized so far (except SlitOR5) as well as two type II PRs (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis and cited literature.

claim: The PR clade contains two type II PRs.
source: One was the so-called PR clade that, as previously observed, contained all type I PRs characterized so far (except SlitOR5) as well as two type II PRs (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis and cited study.

claim: EgriOR31 is a type II PR from the geometrid Ectropis grisescens.
source: The other three lineages harboring PRs consisted of one containing SlitOR5, one containing EgriOR31 (a type II PR from the geometrid Ectropis grisescens; Li et al., 2017) and one containing EsemOR3 and 5 (type 0 PRs from the non-dytrisian moth Eriocrania semipurpurella; Yuvaraj et al., 2017).

claim: EsemOR3 and EsemOR5 are type 0 PRs from the non-dytrisian moth Eriocrania semipurpurella.
source: The other three lineages harboring PRs consisted of one containing SlitOR5, one containing EgriOR31 (a type II PR from the geometrid Ectropis grisescens; Li et al., 2017) and one containing EsemOR3 and 5 (type 0 PRs from the non-dytrisian moth Eriocrania semipurpurella; Yuvaraj et al., 2017).

claim: Most sex-biased lepidopteran ORs identified to date cluster within the PR clade and the lineage containing SlitOR5.
source: Interestingly, most sex-biased lepidopteran ORs identified to date clustered within the PR clade and the lineage containing SlitOR5.

claim: Sex-biased ORs within the PR clade are mainly male-biased.
source: While sex-biased ORs within the PR clade were mainly male-biased, the SlitOR5 lineage contained an equal proportion of male and female-biased receptors, identified from species belonging to different families of Lepidoptera.

claim: The SlitOR5 lineage contains an equal proportion of male and female-biased receptors.
source: While sex-biased ORs within the PR clade were mainly male-biased, the SlitOR5 lineage contained an equal proportion of male and female-biased receptors, identified from species belonging to different families of Lepidoptera.

claim: The SlitOR5 lineage contains receptors from species belonging to different families of Lepidoptera.
source: While sex-biased ORs within the PR clade were mainly male-biased, the SlitOR5 lineage contained an equal proportion of male and female-biased receptors, identified from species belonging to different families of Lepidoptera.

claim: The PR clade and the SlitOR5 lineage are more closely related to clades harboring receptors for plant volatiles than to each other.
source: Deep nodes within the phylogeny were highly supported by the bootstrap analysis, enabling us to state that these two PR-containing clades were more closely related to clades harboring receptors for plant volatiles than to each other.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis with bootstrap support.

claim: Receptors tuned to type I pheromone compounds emerged twice independently during the evolution of Lepidoptera.
source: This suggests that receptors tuned to type I pheromone compounds emerged twice independently during the evolution of Lepidoptera, and that the clade containing SlitOR5 may constitute a novel lineage of candidate PRs.
evidence: Inference from phylogenetic analysis and functional data.

claim: The clade containing SlitOR5 may constitute a novel lineage of candidate PRs.
source: This suggests that receptors tuned to type I pheromone compounds emerged twice independently during the evolution of Lepidoptera, and that the clade containing SlitOR5 may constitute a novel lineage of candidate PRs.
evidence: Inference from phylogenetic and functional data.

claim: 75% of all known moth sex pheromone compounds belong to type I.
source: 75% of all known moth sex pheromone compounds belong to type I and are straight-chain acetates, alcohols or aldehydes with 10 to 18 carbon atoms (Ando et al., 2004).

claim: Type I pheromones are straight-chain acetates, alcohols or aldehydes with 10 to 18 carbon atoms.
source: 75% of all known moth sex pheromone compounds belong to type I and are straight-chain acetates, alcohols or aldehydes with 10 to 18 carbon atoms (Ando et al., 2004).

claim: Type I pheromones have been found in most moth families investigated.
source: Type I pheromones have been found in most moth families investigated, whereas the other types are restricted to only a few families (Löfstedt et al., 2016).

claim: Type 0, II, and III pheromones are restricted to only a few moth families.
source: Type I pheromones have been found in most moth families investigated, whereas the other types are restricted to only a few families (Löfstedt et al., 2016).

claim: Four types of sex pheromones have been described in moths (types 0, I, II and III).
source: Four types of sex pheromones have been described in moths (types 0, I, II and III), with distinct chemical structures and biosynthetic pathways (Löfstedt et al., 2016).

claim: The four types of moth sex pheromones have distinct chemical structures and biosynthetic pathways.
source: Four types of sex pheromones have been described in moths (types 0, I, II and III), with distinct chemical structures and biosynthetic pathways (Löfstedt et al., 2016).

claim: Each type of OSN usually expresses one pheromone receptor responsible for signal transduction.
source: Each type of OSN usually expresses one pheromone receptor (PR) responsible for signal transduction.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of insect olfactory system.

claim: PRs are 7-transmembrane domain proteins belonging to the odorant receptor family.
source: PRs are 7-transmembrane domain proteins belonging to the odorant receptor (OR) family and, as ORs, are co-expressed in OSNs together with the conserved co-receptor Orco (Chertemps, 2017; Fleischer and Krieger, 2018).

claim: PRs are co-expressed in OSNs together with the conserved co-receptor Orco.
source: PRs are 7-transmembrane domain proteins belonging to the odorant receptor (OR) family and, as ORs, are co-expressed in OSNs together with the conserved co-receptor Orco (Chertemps, 2017; Fleischer and Krieger, 2018).

claim: Most type I PRs appeared to be specific to only one compound.
source: Since the first discovery of moth PRs (Krieger et al., 2004; Sakurai et al., 2004), numerous pheromone receptors tuned to type I pheromone compounds have been characterized through different hererologous expression systems, and most appeared to be specific to only one compound (Zhang and Löfstedt, 2015).

claim: Type I PRs belong to a dedicated monophyletic subfamily of ORs called the 'PR clade'.
source: Type I PRs belong to a dedicated monophyletic subfamily of ORs, the so-called 'PR clade', suggesting a unique emergence early in the evolution of Lepidoptera (Yuvaraj et al., 2018).

claim: The PR clade suggests a unique emergence early in the evolution of Lepidoptera.
source: Type I PRs belong to a dedicated monophyletic subfamily of ORs, the so-called 'PR clade', suggesting a unique emergence early in the evolution of Lepidoptera (Yuvaraj et al., 2018).

claim: Type I PRs exhibit male-biased expression.
source: Another hallmark of type I PRs is their male-biased expression (Koenig et al., 2015).

claim: Phylogenetic position and expression pattern have been the main criteria used to select candidate PRs for functional studies.
source: The phylogenetic position and the expression pattern have thus been the main criteria used to select candidate PRs for functional studies.
evidence: Statement about research methodology in the field.

claim: S. littoralis is a polyphagous crop pest that uses type I sex pheromone compounds.
source: Likewise, we selected PRs from the male transcriptome of the cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis (Legeai et al., 2011), a polyphagous crop pest that uses type I sex pheromone compounds (Muñoz et al., 2008) and that has been established as a model in insect chemical ecology (Ljungberg et al., 1993; Binyameen et al., 2012; Saveer et al., 2012; Poivet et al., 2012; de Fouchier et al., 2017).

claim: S. littoralis has been established as a model in insect chemical ecology.
source: Likewise, we selected PRs from the male transcriptome of the cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis (Legeai et al., 2011), a polyphagous crop pest that uses type I sex pheromone compounds (Muñoz et al., 2008) and that has been established as a model in insect chemical ecology (Ljungberg et al., 1993; Binyameen et al., 2012; Saveer et al., 2012; Poivet et al., 2012; de Fouchier et al., 2017).

claim: Two PRs tuned to minor components of the S. littoralis pheromone blend were characterized through heterologous expression.
source: Through heterologous expression, we characterized two PRs tuned to minor components of the S. littoralis pheromone blend (Montagné et al., 2012; de Fouchier et al., 2015), but none of the tested candidate PRs detected the major pheromone component (Z,E)-9,11-tetradecadienyl acetate (hereafter referred as (Z,E)-9,11-14:OAc), which is necessary and sufficient to elicit all steps of the male mate-seeking behavioral sequence (Quero et al., 1996).

claim: (Z,E)-9,11-14:OAc is necessary and sufficient to elicit all steps of the male mate-seeking behavioral sequence in S. littoralis.
source: Through heterologous expression, we characterized two PRs tuned to minor components of the S. littoralis pheromone blend (Montagné et al., 2012; de Fouchier et al., 2015), but none of the tested candidate PRs detected the major pheromone component (Z,E)-9,11-tetradecadienyl acetate (hereafter referred as (Z,E)-9,11-14:OAc), which is necessary and sufficient to elicit all steps of the male mate-seeking behavioral sequence (Quero et al., 1996).

claim: SlitOR5 was the most abundant OR in S. littoralis male antennae.
source: Furthermore, a recent RNAseq analysis showed that SlitOR5 was the most abundant OR in S. littoralis male antennae (Walker et al., 2019).

claim: SlitOR5 is highly expressed in male antennae.
source: Notably, a preliminary analysis of S. littoralis OR expression patterns led to the identification of such a receptor, SlitOR5, which was highly expressed in male antennae but did not belong to the PR clade (Legeai et al., 2011).

claim: SlitOR5 does not belong to the PR clade.
source: Notably, a preliminary analysis of S. littoralis OR expression patterns led to the identification of such a receptor, SlitOR5, which was highly expressed in male antennae but did not belong to the PR clade (Legeai et al., 2011).

claim: LT1A OSNs are known to detect (Z,E)-9,11-14:OAc.
source: We compared the response spectra of heterologously expressed SlitOR5 with that of S. littoralis male OSNs housed in type one long trichoid sensilla (LT1A OSNs, Figure 2C), known to detect (Z,E)-9,11-14:OAc (Ljungberg et al., 1993; Quero et al., 1996).

claim: Seven G0 individuals carrying at least one mutation in SlitOr5 were identified from 66 genotyped hatched larvae.
source: We genotyped 66 G0 hatched larvae and found seven individuals carrying at least one mutation in SlitOr5.
evidence: Supported by genotyping data from CRISPR/Cas9 experiment.

claim: More than one thousand eggs were injected with guide RNAs and Cas9 protein for CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing.
source: Guide RNAs were injected along with the Cas9 protein in more than one thousand eggs.

claim: Within the SlitOR5 lineage, almost half of the sex-biased ORs were female-biased (13 out of 28).
source: Conversely, within the SlitOR5 lineage, almost half of the sex-biased ORs were female-biased (13 out of 28, compared to 4 out of 63 in the classical PR clade).

claim: Within the classical PR clade, 4 out of 63 sex-biased ORs were female-biased.
source: Conversely, within the SlitOR5 lineage, almost half of the sex-biased ORs were female-biased (13 out of 28, compared to 4 out of 63 in the classical PR clade).

claim: Female-biased ORs have been generally proposed to be involved in the detection of plant-emitted oviposition cues.
source: Female-biased ORs have been generally proposed to be involved in the detection of plant-emitted oviposition cues, as demonstrated in Bombyx mori (Anderson et al., 2009).

claim: Female-biased ORs could be tuned to male sex pheromones.
source: However, another interesting hypothesis is that they could be tuned to male sex pheromones.

claim: Male pheromones in moths are involved in various mating behaviors such as female attraction, female acceptance, aggregation of males to form leks, mate assessment or inhibition of other males.
source: In moths, little attention has been put on male pheromones, which are known to be involved in various mating behaviors such as female attraction, female acceptance, aggregation of males to form leks, mate assessment or inhibition of other males (reviewed in Conner and Iyengar, 2016).

claim: The use of male pheromone systems has been selected multiple times in distinct moth families.
source: The use of male pheromone systems has been selected multiple times in distinct moth families, as reflected by the chemical diversity of male pheromone compounds and of the disseminating structures (Birch et al., 1990; Phelan, 1997; Conner and Iyengar, 2016).

claim: The polyphyletic nature of male pheromones would result in a large diversity of female PR types.
source: It is thus expected that this polyphyletic nature of male pheromones would result in a large diversity of female PR types.
evidence: Inference from the polyphyletic nature of male pheromones.

claim: The most common male-emitted volatiles are plant-derived pheromones.
source: Although the most common male-emitted volatiles are plant-derived pheromones (Conner and Iyengar, 2016), some male courtship pheromones are long-chained hydrocarbons related to type I female pheromone compounds (Hillier and Vickers, 2004) that could be detected by female-biased type I PRs such as those identified within the SlitOR5 lineage.

claim: Some male courtship pheromones are long-chained hydrocarbons related to type I female pheromone compounds.
source: Although the most common male-emitted volatiles are plant-derived pheromones (Conner and Iyengar, 2016), some male courtship pheromones are long-chained hydrocarbons related to type I female pheromone compounds (Hillier and Vickers, 2004) that could be detected by female-biased type I PRs such as those identified within the SlitOR5 lineage.

claim: The ancestral protein from which the PR clade arose is thought to be an OR tuned to plant-emitted volatiles.
source: The ancestral protein from which the so-called 'PR clade' would have arisen is thought to be an OR tuned to plant-emitted volatiles (Yuvaraj et al., 2017; Yuvaraj et al., 2018).

claim: PRs for Type 0 group in distinct paralogous lineages unrelated to the PR clade.
source: Together with the findings that PRs for Type 0 (Yuvaraj et al., 2017) and one PR for type II pheromones (Li et al., 2017) group in distinct paralogous lineages also unrelated to the PR clade, our data suggest that lepidopteran PRs have evolved four times in four paralogous lineages.
evidence: Supported by cited studies and current data.

claim: One PR for type II pheromones groups in a distinct paralogous lineage unrelated to the PR clade.
source: Together with the findings that PRs for Type 0 (Yuvaraj et al., 2017) and one PR for type II pheromones (Li et al., 2017) group in distinct paralogous lineages also unrelated to the PR clade, our data suggest that lepidopteran PRs have evolved four times in four paralogous lineages.
evidence: Supported by cited study and current data.

claim: Lepidopteran PRs have evolved four times in four paralogous lineages.
source: Together with the findings that PRs for Type 0 (Yuvaraj et al., 2017) and one PR for type II pheromones (Li et al., 2017) group in distinct paralogous lineages also unrelated to the PR clade, our data suggest that lepidopteran PRs have evolved four times in four paralogous lineages.
evidence: Inference from phylogenetic analysis and cited studies.

claim: No OR tuned to plant volatiles has been identified in lineages closely related to the SlitOR5 lineage.
source: Yet, no OR tuned to plant volatiles has been identified in closely related lineages.

claim: Changes in sex pheromone communication are expected to play a major role in the rise of reproductive barriers and the emergence of new species.
source: The use of pheromone signals for mate recognition is widespread in animals, and changes in sex pheromone communication are expected to play a major role in the rise of reproductive barriers and the emergence of new species (Smadja and Butlin, 2009).

claim: Moths have been a preferred taxon for pheromone research since the first chemical identification of a pheromone in Bombyx mori.
source: Since the first chemical identification of such a pheromone in Bombyx mori (Butenandt et al., 1959), moths (Insecta, Lepidoptera) have been a preferred taxon for pheromone research (Cardé and Haynes, 2004; Kaissling, 2014).

claim: The diversification of pheromone signals has likely played a prominent role in the extensive radiation observed in Lepidoptera.
source: The diversification of pheromone signals has likely played a prominent role in the extensive radiation observed in Lepidoptera, which represents almost 10% of the total described species of living organisms (Stork, 2018).

claim: Lepidoptera represents almost 10% of the total described species of living organisms.
source: The diversification of pheromone signals has likely played a prominent role in the extensive radiation observed in Lepidoptera, which represents almost 10% of the total described species of living organisms (Stork, 2018).

claim: Female moths generally release a species-specific blend of volatile molecules which attract males over a long distance.
source: Female moths generally release a species-specific blend of volatile molecules, which attract males over a long distance (Cardé and Haynes, 2004).

claim: Two ORs from Ctenopseustis obliquana and C. herana have been functionally studied by heterologous expression in cell cultures, but no ligand could be identified.
source: Among these, two ORs from Ctenopseustis obliquana and C. herana (Tortricidae) have been functionally studied by heterologous expression in cell cultures, but no ligand could be identified (Steinwender et al., 2015).

claim: In Dendrolimus species, there is no OR clustering in the PR clade.
source: In the Lasiocampidae species Dendrolimus punctatus, these male-biased ORs have been referred to as 'Dendrolimus-specific odorant receptors', with the suspicion that they would represent good PR candidates since in Dendrolimus species, there is no OR clustering in the PR clade (Zhang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).

claim: Male-biased ORs in Dendrolimus punctatus have been referred to as 'Dendrolimus-specific odorant receptors'.
source: In the Lasiocampidae species Dendrolimus punctatus, these male-biased ORs have been referred to as 'Dendrolimus-specific odorant receptors', with the suspicion that they would represent good PR candidates since in Dendrolimus species, there is no OR clustering in the PR clade (Zhang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).

claim: BmorOR30 belongs to the SlitOR5 lineage but no ligand could be identified for it.
source: However, most remain orphan ORs, including BmorOR30 that does belong to the SlitOR5 lineage but for which no ligand could be identified (Anderson et al., 2009).

claim: The phylogenetic analysis included entire OR repertoires from nine species, each belonging to a different lepidopteran superfamily.
source: The dataset of lepidopteran amino acid OR sequences used to build the phylogeny shown in Figure 1 included entire OR repertoires from the following nine species, each belonging to a different lepidopteran superfamily: Bombyx mori (Bombycoidea; Tanaka et al., 2009), Dendrolimus punctatus (Lasiocampoidea; Zhang et al., 2017), Ectropis grisescens (Geometroidea; Li et al., 2017), Epiphyas postvittana (Tortricoidea; Corcoran et al., 2015), Eriocrania semipurpurella (Eriocranioidea; Yuvaraj et al., 2017), Heliconius melpomene (Papilionoidea; Heliconius Genome Consortium, 2012), Ostrinia furnacalis (Pyraloidea; Yang et al., 2015), Plutella xylostella (Yponomeutoidea; Engsontia et al., 2014) and Spodoptera littoralis (Noctuoidea; Walker et al., 2019).

claim: The phylogenetic analysis identified 20 paralogous OR lineages.
source: Among the 20 paralogous lineages identified (each having evolved in principle from an ancestral OR present in the last common ancestor of Lepidoptera), SlitOR5 belonged to a lineage distantly related to the type I PR clade, as well as to the lineages containing type 0 and type II PRs (Figure 1B).

claim: Each paralogous lineage has evolved in principle from an ancestral OR present in the last common ancestor of Lepidoptera.
source: Among the 20 paralogous lineages identified (each having evolved in principle from an ancestral OR present in the last common ancestor of Lepidoptera), SlitOR5 belonged to a lineage distantly related to the type I PR clade, as well as to the lineages containing type 0 and type II PRs (Figure 1B).
evidence: Inference about evolutionary origin of OR lineages.

claim: The large clade containing SlitOR5 and PR-containing lineages has been previously shown to contain ORs tuned to terpenes and aliphatic molecules.
source: This clade has been previously shown to contain ORs tuned to terpenes and aliphatic molecules – including sex pheromones – and exhibits higher evolutionary rates compared to more ancient clades that contain many receptors for aromatics (de Fouchier et al., 2017).

claim: The large clade containing SlitOR5 and PR-containing lineages exhibits higher evolutionary rates compared to more ancient clades that contain many receptors for aromatics.
source: This clade has been previously shown to contain ORs tuned to terpenes and aliphatic molecules – including sex pheromones – and exhibits higher evolutionary rates compared to more ancient clades that contain many receptors for aromatics (de Fouchier et al., 2017).

claim: SlitOR5 was expressed in Drosophila melanogaster OSNs housed in at1 trichoid sensilla in place of the endogenous PR DmelOR67d.
source: First, we expressed SlitOR5 in Drosophila melanogaster OSNs housed in at1 trichoid sensilla, in place of the endogenous PR DmelOR67d (Kurtovic et al., 2007).

claim: Male-biased ORs have been found in Lasiocampidae, Sphingidae, Noctuidae and Tortricidae within the SlitOR5 lineage.
source: Notably, male-biased ORs have been found in Lasiocampidae, Sphingidae, Noctuidae and Tortricidae.

claim: At least one moth PR does not belong to the classical PR subfamily but to a distantly related OR lineage.
source: Here, using a combination of heterologous expression and in vivo genome editing methods, we bring functional evidence that at least one moth PR does not belong to this subfamily but to a distantly related OR lineage.
evidence: Main finding of the study based on functional data.

claim: The functional data suggest two independent apparitions of PRs tuned to type I pheromones in Lepidoptera.
source: Together with a comprehensive phylogenetic analysis of moth ORs, our functional data suggest two independent apparitions of PRs tuned to type I pheromones in Lepidoptera, opening up a new path for studying the evolution of moth pheromone communication.
evidence: Inference from functional and phylogenetic data.
